title: The queen in a busy position (part 1 of 4)
sources: rules of chess (python-chess legal move generation, via tools/validate.py)
docs/citable-views.md: no external view is attributed in this lesson; the rule-of-thumb statements are labelled [H] and [I]
provenance: the three opening boards replay 1.e4 e5 2.Qh5 Nc6 3.Bc4 with python-chess; the other positions are authored and validated

steps.text: By the end you can explain how the queen moves, what stops her, and how a queen is trapped or lost in three moves. First, try a position cold: tap every square she can reach.

That was the **queen**: a rook and a bishop in one piece. She has **eight lines**, four straight and four slanting, and she slides along each over empty squares, as far as she likes. Not sure how you did? Good. The next boards are a worked example, so look first, then try again.

steps.caption: The piece on c3 is a queen. Her pawn on e3 and king on e1 stop two lines one square early. The knight on d5 is on none of her lines (it does attack her, which is the next chapter).

line.say: The queen slides up and to the left along a diagonal, over empty squares, to a5.
Black moves the king; we are only watching the queen.

claims.statement: These are exactly the squares the queen on c3 can move to.

steps.caption: This is the position you tried. Seven lines are open, 24 squares in all. White's own pawn on f3 shuts the eighth line at once.

line.say: She glides up and to the left, over empty squares, as far as b7.

claims.statement: These are exactly the squares the queen on e4 can move to.

steps.caption: From a1 she reaches 21 squares; from d4 on an empty board 27, because all eight lines run across the board. A corner costs her few squares but five of her eight lines.

line.say: She steps to the middle: now all eight lines run across the board.
Black's king moves; the queen is the one being studied.

claims.statement: These are exactly the squares the queen on a1 can move to.

steps.text: Every line ends by itself. An **own piece** is a wall: she stops on the square before it. An **enemy piece** is the last square of the line: she may take it, and then she stops there. She never hops over either kind. Watch both on the next two boards.

steps.caption: Her own pawn closes the long diagonal at d4. The other lines from a1 stay open.

line.say: She slides along the diagonal and stops one square before her own pawn.
Black's king moves; nothing else changes.

claims.statement: Her own pawn stands on d4.
She cannot hop over her own pawn.
The file upward is still open.
The first rank is still open.

steps.caption: An enemy pawn on d4 is the last square of that diagonal. She may take it, but not go past it.

line.say: She captures the pawn and stops on its square.

claims.statement: The pawn on d4 ends the line, so e5 is out of reach.

steps.text: A blocker closes **one** line; the other seven stay open unless she is pinned or her king is in check (both come later). So when a piece stands next to her, count the lines again, one by one. *Rule of thumb:* eight lines, each checked on its own.

steps.caption: A white pawn on c4 shuts the line straight up. Look at what is still open: seven lines, 20 squares.

line.say: The diagonal toward e5 is as open as it ever was.

claims.statement: These are exactly the squares the queen on c3 can move to.
Her own pawn on c4 is in the way.

steps.caption: A lone queen can use all three kinds of slide. Here she makes one of each, and the kings stay out of the way.

line.say: Straight up the file, like a rook.
Straight along the rank, also like a rook.
Along a diagonal, like a bishop: the third kind of slide.

claims.statement: e3 is on none of her lines.

steps.text: **Remember.** The queen is a rook and a bishop in one piece, with eight lines. Check each line on its own. Her own piece is a wall, so she stops one square short. An enemy piece is the last square of that line: she may take it, then stops. One blocker closes only one line; the others stay open.
